title: Felix and the Haywire Magic
markdown:
Dawn broke over the Grand Majestic Theatre. Colours found the rooftops. A pigeon applauded itself on the gutter. Felix Flicker sprang from bed as if the floor had issued an invitation. Today tasted of fizzy lemonade and warm toast. Sun striped the floorboards. He tugged on his favourite jumper, the peppermint-striped one that always seemed to add pep, and took the stairs two at a time.

Downstairs Uncle Magnus packed top hats and trick boxes, silk scarves, a dove that was (usually) only a dove. “Morning!” Felix chirped, voice bubbling like a brand-new day.

Uncle Magnus, whose smile could light up any backstage, winked. “Indeed, my boy. The Grand Opening Gala. A night for gasps and giggles. First, a tiny test spell, perfectly, absolutely perfect. You’ll help, won’t you, Felix?”

Felix practically leaped. He grabbed his lucky rabbit’s foot — soft felt, still lucky — and dashed toward the immense dusty velvet curtains. As he pushed through, a tinkling giggle floated to him.

“Psst. Over here.”

Cora Cobweb, the theatre’s resident ghost, shimmered misty blue, as if she had just floated out of a fluffy cloud. She was Felix’s most secret friend. Nobody else could see her, which made their adventures extra theirs.

“Today’s the big show,” Felix whispered.

“The whole house is buzzing.” Cora did a spectral flip. “He’s getting the wand out. Watch.”

Uncle Magnus stood centre stage, moustache twitching. He pointed a glittery, star-tipped wand at a pile of props. “Let these make-believe wonders become their true selves for a moment. A quick test.”

Whoosh.

A tiger padded on, stripes bright orange and black, golden eyes blinking. It flicked its tail and rumbled, looking at Felix as if he might be breakfast or a very small usher.

“That’s not fake,” Cora whispered, flickering. “That’s a real, live, grumpy tiger.”

Felix’s heart gave a determined thump. This was not the planned rehearsal. Then zap: a dark puffy storm cloud crackled with tiny lightning and began to drip, drip, drip a fine mist onto the polished floor.

“Not a downpour,” Magnus said, wiping his nose. “A gentle mist. That was the idea.”

Crash. A pirate ship creaked at the stage edge, timbers complaining, Jolly Roger flapping, tattered sails billowing as if a sea had borrowed the wings. A brightly coloured parrot squawked from the crow’s nest. A gruff voice demanded boarding.

The audience would arrive in less than an hour. Ticket holders. Programmes. Expectation.

“Haywire,” Magnus said. “Far too real.”

Cora zoomed past Felix’s ear. “A proper adventure.”

Felix looked at her, then at the tiger sniffing the damp boards, then at the ship. “We have to fix this. Uncle Magnus can’t do it alone. Wings of my wings, Cora — we keep this stage.”

“Felix notices everything,” Cora told Magnus. “I can float where you can’t.”

Felix’s keen eyes darted. He spotted a large plush velvet cushion in the wings, the sort used for fainting sopranos and lucky cats. “Tiger. Is that your favourite napping spot? Soft. Cozy.” The tiger blinked, tilted its head, then padded over with surprising quiet and flopped down with a contented rumble. Phew. One problem, sorted into sleep.

The cloud still drizzled, making little puddles that reflected the flies. “Cora. A big fluffy stage blanket. Something we could tuck a cloud into.”

Cora zipped off like a tiny rocket and shoved one back, huge and soft as a sleeping field.

Then came the silent work. No chatter. Only the drip, the rustle of wool, Felix jumping to catch a corner, Cora herding mist into cloth as if tucking in weather. They gathered the difficult materials — cushion, blanket, later canvas — as if they were rare herbs from a wood. The cloud grumbled like distant thunder and settled into a sleeping fluffball. The puddles stopped growing.

The parrot squawked for plunder.

“What did you mean the ship to be?” Felix asked.

“An illusion,” Magnus said. “Painted backdrop. Waves. A foghorn.”

They fled into the wild wood of backstage: rope forests, paint-smelling flats, a moon made of wood. Felix rummaged through rolled canvases, Cora flitting, until he found a night sky thick with painted stars. “This. Sailing across the dark.”

They unfurled it toward the ship, a lot of effort and four hands if you counted ghost ones. Canvas and timber seemed to agree. The ship sank into blues and glints until it was only a clever part of the painted night. The parrot gave one bewildered squawk and settled, plunder postponed.

The heavy doors creaked. That was the deadline, public as a trial: the first audience, murmur of coats and programmes, the usher’s cough. Felix grinned at Cora and at Magnus. The tiger snored on velvet. The cloud was a peaceful lump under its blanket, silent. The ship was stars.

The wand, which had caused all the unfair realness, lay quiet on the prop table, its little star looking almost sheepish. Proportionate enough.

“Wings of my wings,” Cora whispered, bouncing, another spectral flip. “We kept it.”

Magnus clapped Felix’s shoulder, eyes shining. “Brave and clever. You saved the show.”

Felix felt a glow brighter than any footlight. He looked at the stage, ready for the gala, almost perfect, which was better than haywire. He looked at Cora, friend of the same curtain, same side of the dark. Family of the wings, if you liked.

“Wings of my wings,” he said, and grinned. “Today is going to be amazing.” The adventure was just beginning.
characters: Felix (the stage magician's nephew), Cora (a backstage ghost)
